metadata.title: Adaptive model predictive control with exploring property for constrained linear systems that uses basis function model parametrization

extraction_notes.note: The displayed equation completing each of these sentences has no closing punctuation and runs straight into the next sentence, so the prose node ends at the colon before the display; the equation (EP12, EP21, EP30) is a separate node tied by a uses edge.

Uncited standard facts about orthonormal basis expansions (expansion of a stable transfer function, coefficients as projections); typed claim with origin external rather than definition or theorem, since the paper names no result.
Lemma 5.1 is taken from Bai, Tempo & Cho and has no proof here, so it is origin external although it sits in a lemma environment.
Results asserted in running text with no or only a one-clause justification; kept as claims (or a remark) with rigor semi_formal rather than as unjustified prose.
Two eqnarray blocks carry two printed numbers each ((7)-(8) and (56)-(57)); each is one equation fact, so one equation node, and both labels resolve to it.

Motivational prose (Sec. 1, the start of Sec. 4 and Sec. 5), the initialization remarks for H_c(0) and Phi(1|0), the advice on choosing a near the dominant pole, and the one-line remark on Kautz-case matrices are not separate nodes.

nodes.statement: We denote the vector of control inputs at time step $t\in {\mathbb Z}$ by $u(t)=[u_1(t),\hdots,u_{n_u}(t)]^T$, where $u_i(t)\in {\mathbb R},\,i=1,\hdots,n_u$ are the individual plant inputs at the time step $t$ and $^T$ stands for the matrix transpose operator.

nodes.name: Plant output and output disturbance vectors
nodes.statement: In addition, we denote the vector of plant outputs by $y(t)=[y_1(t),\hdots,y_{n_y}(t)]^T$, where $y_j(t)\in {\mathbb R} ,\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ are the individual plant outputs, and we denote the vector of output disturbances by $d(t)=[d_1(t),\hdots,d_{n_y}(t)]^T$, where each $d_j(t)\in {\mathbb R}, \, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ denotes the contribution of the disturbances to the output $j$ at time step $t$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduces the plant output vector $y(t)$ and the output disturbance vector $d(t)$.

nodes.name: Basis function parametrization of the plant
nodes.statement: The dynamic relation between the plant inputs and each of the plant outputs $y_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$, is given by: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} y_j(t)&=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n_u}\sum\limits_{k=1}^{m}h_{ji}(k)\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u_i(t)\right)+d_j(t)= H_j^T\varphi(t)+d_j(t), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),\, k=1,\hdots, m$ are the basis transfer functions defined by the parameter $a$ that are selected by the control designer, $q$ is the time shift operator ($qu(t)\doteq u(t+1)$) and the operator $\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u(t)\right)$ denotes the output of a linear system represented by the transfer function $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ at the time step $t$, when the signal $u$ is applied as its input: \begin{equation} \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q),u(t)\right)\doteq \sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi_k(a,l)u(t-l), \end{equation} where $\Psi_k(a,l)$ are the impulse response coefficients of the basis function $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each output is a linear combination of basis-filtered inputs plus disturbance; basis transfer functions $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ act via their impulse responses.

nodes.name: Regressor vector and modeling coefficients
nodes.statement: $\varphi(t)\doteq [\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_1(a,q)u_1(t)\right), \hdots,\\\zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_m(a,q)u_1(t)\right),\hdots, \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_1(a,q)u_{n_u}(t)\right), \hdots, \zeta\left(\mathcal{L}_m(a,q)u_{n_u}(t)\right)]^T$ is the regressor vector and each of the vectors $H_j\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um},\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ contains $n_ym$ modeling coefficients needed to describe the influence of all the control inputs on the plant output $j$: $H_j\doteq[h_{j1}(1), \hdots, h_{j1}(m), \hdots, h_{jn_u}(1), \hdots, h_{jn_u}(m)]^T$.
nodes.statement_short: Regressor $\varphi(t)$ stacks basis-filtered inputs; $H_j$ stacks the coefficients for output $j$.

nodes.name: Coefficient matrix H
nodes.statement: By defining the matrix $H\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y\times n_um}$ as $H \doteq \left[H_1, \hdots, H_{n_y}\right]^T$, the dependence of the plant output on the regressor and the disturbance vectors can be written as: \begin{equation} y(t)=H\varphi(t)+d(t). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Common basis parameter and order for all channels
nodes.statement: Note that the same value of the parameter $a$ and the number of modeling coefficients $m$ is assumed for all the input-output pairs, in order to simplify the notation. All the results can easily be extended to the case when different values for $a$ and $m$ are assumed for each input-output pair.
nodes.label: R:different

nodes.name: Measured plant output
nodes.statement: The measured output available for feedback control is corrupted by noise. In particular, the vector of measured plant outputs is given as: \begin{equation} \tilde{y}(t)=y(t)+v(t), \end{equation} where $v(t)=[v_1(t),\hdots,v_{n_y}(t)]^T$ and $v_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ are the individual measurement noise terms that affect each of the measured plant outputs.

nodes.name: Prior assumption on disturbance and noise
nodes.statement: (Prior assumption on disturbance and noise) $d$ and $v$ are bounded as: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{lll} |d_j(t)|&\leq&\epsilon_{d_j}\\ |v_j(t)|&\leq&\epsilon_{v_j} \end{array},\,\forall t\in{\mathbb Z},\,\forall j=1,\hdots,n_y, \end{equation} where $\epsilon_{d_j}$ and $\epsilon_{v_j}$ are positive scalars.\
nodes.label: A:disturbance

nodes.name: Vector disturbance and noise bounds
nodes.statement: We also use the noise and disturbance magnitude bounds in the vector notation as $\epsilon_d=[\epsilon_{d_1}, \hdots, \epsilon_{d_{n_y}}]^T$ and $\epsilon_v=[\epsilon_{v_1}, \hdots, \epsilon_{v_{n_y}}]^T$.

nodes.name: Prior assumption on the system (initial polytopic model set)
nodes.statement: (Prior assumption on the system) The plant belongs to the following model set: $H\in \mathcal{F}(0)$, with \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}(0) \doteq \left\{H\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y\times n_um}: A_{j}(0)H_j\leq b_{j}(0), j=1,\hdots, n_y \right\}, \end{equation} where the inequalities in \eqref{Eq:system_set} should be interpreted as element-wise inequalities and each matrix $A_{j}(0)\in {\mathbb R}^{r_{j}(0)\times n_um}$ and vector $b_{j}(0) \in {\mathbb R}^{r_{j}(0)}$ define a close and convex set, i.e. a polytope with $r_{j}(0)$ faces.
nodes.label: A:system_class

nodes.name: Constrained tracking and disturbance rejection control objective
nodes.statement: Under Assumptions \ref{A:disturbance} and \ref{A:system_class}, the goal is to control the plant in order to track a desired output reference and reject disturbances from $t=0$ up to some finite time step $T$, where the time horizon $T$ can be very large ($T\gg m$). In addition, we assume that the control inputs $u(l), l=-T_1,\hdots,-1$ are known, where the horizon $T_1$ should be long enough such that the effects of $u(-T_1-1)$ on the regressor vector $\varphi(0)$ are small. The error in the regressor vector coming from the initial state can be accounted for by embedding it in the bound on $d(t)$. Moreover, the controller shall enforce input and output constraints. Such a control objective can be formalized by the following optimization problem: \begin{eqnarray} & \begin{aligned} \min\limits_{u(0),\hdots,u(T-1)}\sum_{t=0}^{T} &\left( y(t)-y_{\text{des}}(t) \right)^TQ \left( y(t)-y_{\text{des}}(t) \right)+u(t)^T S u(t) + \Delta u(t)^T R \Delta u(t) \end{aligned}\\ &\begin{aligned} & \text{subject to},\,\forall t\in[0,T] \\ &\begin{array}{lllll} Cu(t)&\leq &g\\ L \Delta u(t)&\leq&f\\ E y(t)&\leq& p \end{array} \end{aligned} \end{eqnarray} where $y_{\text{des}}(t)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y}$ is the desired output reference, $Q \in {\mathbb R}^{n_y\times n_y}$, $S\in {\mathbb R}^{n_u\times n_u}$ and $R \in {\mathbb R}^{n_u \times n_u}$ are positive semi-definite weighting matrices selected by the control designer, and $\Delta u(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ is the rate of change of the control input. The element-wise inequalities in \eqref{Eq:IO_constraints} define convex sets through the matrices $C\in{\mathbb R}^{n_i\times n_u}$, $L\in{\mathbb R}^{n_{\Delta_u}\times n_u}$, $E\in{\mathbb R}^{n_o\times n_y}$ and the vectors $g\in{\mathbb R}^{n_i}$, $f\in{\mathbb R}^{n_{\Delta_u}}$, $p\in{\mathbb R}^{n_o}$, where $n_i$, $n_{\Delta_u}$ and $n_o$ are the number of linear constraints on the inputs, input rates and outputs, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a quadratic tracking/input/input-rate cost over horizon $T$ subject to linear input, input-rate and output constraints for an uncertain plant.

nodes.name: Known past inputs
nodes.statement: In addition, we assume that the control inputs $u(l), l=-T_1,\hdots,-1$ are known, where the horizon $T_1$ should be long enough such that the effects of $u(-T_1-1)$ on the regressor vector $\varphi(0)$ are small.

nodes.name: Input constraint set assumptions
nodes.statement: We assume that the set defining the constraints on $\Delta u(t)$ contains the origin and that the constraint set of $u(t)$ is compact.

nodes.name: Unmodeled dynamics embedded in the output disturbance
nodes.statement: Note that the influence of the unmodeled dynamics to the plant outputs can be embedded into the output disturbance vector $d(t)$. The facts that the magnitudes of the control inputs are bounded and that the controlled system is stable can be exploited to calculate the bounds on the contribution of the unmodeled dynamics to the plant outputs.
nodes.label: R:IIR

nodes.name: Orthonormal basis function expansion of stable transfer functions
nodes.statement: Any stable transfer function can be represented by the following infinite sum: \begin{equation} G(q)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}h(k)\mathcal{L}_k(a,q), \end{equation} where $q$ is the time shift operator ($qu(t)\doteq u(t+1)$) and $\mathcal{L}_k$ are mutually orthogonal transfer functions characterized by: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2\pi j}\oint \mathcal{L}_p(a,q)\mathcal{L}_k(a,q^{-1})\frac{dq}{q}=\delta_{pk}, \end{equation} where $\delta_{pk}$ is the Kronecker delta function and the integral is around the unit circle. The parameter $a\in \mathbb{C},\, |a|\leq1$ defines the basis functions. The sequence of coefficients $h(k)$ is convergent as $\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}h(k)=0$.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
conclusions: can be represented by the following infinite sum:
The sequence of coefficients $h(k)$ is convergent as $\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}h(k)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: A stable transfer function expands in mutually orthonormal basis functions $\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ with coefficients tending to zero.

nodes.name: Laguerre basis functions
nodes.statement: Basis transfer functions that are usually employed in practice are the Laguerre ones, given as: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}_k(a,q)=\frac{\sqrt{1-a^2}}{q-a}\left[\frac{1-aq}{q-a}\right]^{k-1}, \end{equation} where $a\in {\mathbb R},\, a\in[-1,1]$.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Kautz basis functions
nodes.statement: For systems that exhibit oscillatory behavior, Kautz functions are more appropriate. These functions have the following form: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{2k-1}(a,q)&=\frac{\sqrt{1\!-\!c^2}(q\!-\!b)}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\left[ \frac{-cq^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!+\!1}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\right]^{k\!-\!1}\\ \mathcal{L}_{2k}(a,q)&=\frac{\sqrt{1\!-\!c^2}(1\!-\!b^2)}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\left[ \frac{-cq^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!+\!1}{q^2\!+\!b(c\!-\!1)q\!-\!c}\right]_,^{k\!-\!1} \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $a\in \mathbb{C}, \, |a|\leq1$ and $b=\frac{a+a^*}{1+aa^*}$, $c=-aa^*$ with $^*$ denoting the conjugate of a complex number.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Impulse response basis
nodes.statement: The impulse response model can be regarded as a special case of a basis function parametrization. The basis functions that give rise to an impulse response model are:
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Combined impulse response and Laguerre/Kautz parametrization
nodes.statement: In addition, it is possible to use a parametrization that combines the impulse response and Laguerre or Kautz basis functions. In this case the basis functions are defined as: \begin{equation} \mathcal{L}_k(a,q)=\begin{cases} q^{-k} & \text{if}\, k\leq n\\ \mathcal{B}_{k-n}(a,q)q^{-n} & \text{if}\, k>n \end{cases}, \end{equation} where $\mathcal{B}_k(a,q)$ are the Laguerre or Kautz basis functions as defined in \eqref{Eq:Laguere} and \eqref{Eq:Kautz} and $n$ is another design parameter that determines the number of the impulse response coefficients to be used in the modeling.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Structure of the uncertain transfer function
nodes.statement: We assume that the transfer function from the input $i$ to the output $j$ has the following structure: \begin{equation} G_{ji}(q)=gq^{-\tau}\frac{\prod\limits_{l=1}^{n_z}(q-z_l)}{\prod\limits_{l=1}^{n_p}(q-p_l)}, \end{equation} where $g\in {\mathbb R}$ is the gain, $\tau \in \mathbb{N}$, $\tau \geq 0$ is the transport delay, $Z=[z_1,\hdots,z_{n_z}]^T\in {\mathbb R}^{n_z}$ are the zeros and $P=[p_1,\hdots, p_{n_p}]^T\in {\mathbb R}^{n_p}$ are the poles of the transfer function.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Real poles and zeros for notational simplicity
nodes.statement: Note that real poles and zeros are selected here in order to simplify the notation. All the derivations can be extended to the case of general complex poles and zeros.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Known bounds on gain, delay, zeros and poles
nodes.statement: We assume that the gain, transport delay, poles and zeros are not exactly known, but they belong to the following set: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ccccc} \underline{g}&\leq & g &\leq &\overline{g}\\ \underline{\tau} & \leq & \tau & \leq & \overline{\tau}\\ \underline{Z}&\leq & Z&\leq &\overline{Z}\\ \underline{P} &\leq & P &\leq &\overline{P} \end{array}, \end{equation} where the inequalities in \eqref{Eq:set_of_parameters} should be interpreted as element-wise inequalities and the bounds $\underline{g},\, \overline{g}, \, \underline{\tau}, \, \overline{\tau} \in {\mathbb R}$, $\underline{Z},\, \overline{Z}\in {\mathbb R}^{n_z}$ and $\underline{P},\, \overline{P}\in {\mathbb R}^{n_p}$ are assumed to be known.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Nonnegative delay bound and stable pole bounds
nodes.statement: In addition, it is assumed that $\overline{\tau}\geq 0$ and that the bounds on the poles are selected such that all the poles of the system lay inside the unit circle.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Basis coefficient bounding problem
nodes.statement: Under these assumptions, the goal is, for a given values of parameter $a$ and the model order $m$, to find the upper and lower coefficient bounds $\overline{h}_{ji}(k)$ and $\underline{h}_{ji}(k), \, k=1,\hdots, m$ such that it holds: \begin{equation} \underline{h}_{ji}(k) \leq h_{ji}(k) \leq \overline{h}_{ji}(k), \, k=1,\hdots, m. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Find upper and lower bounds on each basis coefficient $h_{ji}(k)$ valid over the uncertain parameter set.

nodes.name: Impulse response of the uncertain transfer function
nodes.statement: To this end, we denote by $\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l),\, l=1,\hdots, \infty$ the impulse response coefficients of the transfer function \eqref{Eq:Structure1} for different values of $g$, $\tau$, $Z$ and $P$.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Basis coefficients as normalized projections
nodes.statement: Then for any fixed $g$, $\tau$, $Z$ and $P$, the impulse response coefficients $\Psi (g,\tau, Z,P,l)$ can be represented as: \begin{equation} \Psi(g,\!\tau,\!Z,\!P,\!l)=\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}h(g,\!\tau,\!Z,\!P,\!k)\Psi_k(a,\,l), \!\forall l=1,\,\hdots,\, \infty, \end{equation} where, because of the orthogonality of the basis functions, the coefficients $h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)$ are given as normalized projections of $\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l)$ on the impulse responses of the basis functions: \begin{equation} h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)=\frac{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l)\Psi_k(a,l)}{\sum\limits_{l=1}^{\infty}\Psi_k(a,l)^2}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
conclusions: the impulse response coefficients $\Psi (g,\tau, Z,P,l)$ can be represented as:
the coefficients $h(g,\tau,Z,P,k)$ are given as normalized projections of $\Psi(g,\tau,Z,P,l)$ on the impulse responses of the basis functions:
nodes.statement_short: By orthogonality, the basis coefficients of the plant impulse response are its normalized projections on the basis impulse responses.

nodes.name: Contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.statement: The contribution of the unmodeled dynamics on the transfer function from input $i$ to the output $j$ is then given by: \begin{equation} \eta_{ji}(t)=\sum\limits_{k=m+1}^{\infty}h_{ji}(k)\zeta \left(\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)u_i(t)\right). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics

nodes.name: Boundedness of the unmodeled dynamics contribution
nodes.statement: The contribution of the unmodeled dynamics is guaranteed to be bounded: $|\eta(t)|\leq \overline{\eta_{ji}}, \, \forall t$, where the bound $\overline{\eta_{ji}}$ is given by:
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
conclusions: The contribution of the unmodeled dynamics is guaranteed to be bounded: $|\eta(t)|\leq \overline{\eta_{ji}}, \, \forall t$

nodes.name: Approximate computation of the bounds by gridding
nodes.statement: Note that \eqref{Eq:max_u_i} can be computed by solving an LP. However, \eqref{Eq:finding_bounds} and \eqref{Eq:unmodeled_dynamics_bound} are in general very difficult to solve as they are infinite dimensional nonlinear optimization problems. However, the fact that the impulse response coefficients exponentially converge to zero can be used to approximate the infinite sums in \eqref{Eq:Projection} and \eqref{Eq:unmodeled_dynamics_bound} by finite sums of appropriate length. The optimization problems \eqref{Eq:Projection} and \eqref{Eq:unmodeled_dynamics_bound} would then be transformed into finite dimensional optimization problems that could be tackled by griding the box defined in \eqref{Eq:set_of_parameters}. In this approach the values of $h(g,\tau,Z,P,k),\, k=1,\hdots,m$ would be calculated for each of the grid points and the optimization problems could be approximately solved by selecting the grid point that results in the best value of the cost function as the optimum.\\ Such a solution would be suboptimal and the calculated bounds could be further inflated in order to account for the considered approximations.
nodes.section: 3 Selection of the basis functions and estimation of the bounds on the modeling parameter and the contribution of unmodeled dynamics
nodes.statement_short: The bound problems are infinite-dimensional and nonlinear; truncate the sums and grid the parameter box for a suboptimal, inflated solution.

nodes.name: Nominal versus worst-case cost
nodes.statement: Note that an alternative to formulating the cost function based on the tracking error of the nominal model would be to minimize the weighted $l_2$ norm of the worst case tracking error for all the models inside the model set. The drawback of this approach is that if the prior assumptions were not informative enough, the model set would be initially large due to high uncertainty, and then the applied control inputs would be very small in magnitude. Such control inputs would in turn not be very informative, therefore the size of the model set would reduce slowly, hence resulting in a very conservative controller.
nodes.statement_short: A worst-case tracking cost over the model set would give small, uninformative inputs and a conservative controller.
nodes.label: R:why_nominal_model

nodes.name: Adaptive MPC algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[1)]At time step $t$, obtain $\tilde{y}(t)$ and update the model set based on the past applied control inputs and measured plant outputs; \item[2)] Select a nominal model of the plant inside the model set; \item[3)]Calculate a sequence of possible future control inputs by solving a finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) that minimizes the weighted $l_2$ norm of the tracking error for the nominal model and enforces input and output constraints for all the models inside the model set; \item[4)]Apply the first element of the calculated input sequence, set $t=t+1$, go to 1). \end{itemize} \caption{Adaptive MPC algorithm}
nodes.statement_short: Receding-horizon adaptive MPC: update the set-membership model set, pick a nominal model, solve a robust FHOCP, apply the first input.
nodes.label: Alg:RHCOP2

nodes.name: Collected input-output data
nodes.statement: We denote the sequence of the input-output data collected up to time step $t$ as: \begin{equation} \{\varphi(l),\,\tilde{y}(l)\}_{l=0}^{t}, \end{equation} where $\varphi(l)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um}$ is the regressor vector formed by the control inputs applied up to time step $l-1$, and $\tilde{y}(l)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y}$ is the corresponding measured plant output.

nodes.name: Recursive computation of the regressor
nodes.statement: The regressor vector $\varphi(l)$ can be calculated recursively as: \begin{equation} \varphi(l)=W\varphi(l-1)+Zu(l-1), \end{equation} where $W\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um \times n_um}$ and $Z \in {\mathbb R}^{n_um\times n_u}$ are suitable matrices that depend on the selected basis function parametrization.
assumptions: $W\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um \times n_um}$ and $Z \in {\mathbb R}^{n_um\times n_u}$ are suitable matrices that depend on the selected basis function parametrization
conclusions: The regressor vector $\varphi(l)$ can be calculated recursively as:

nodes.name: Model set F(t)
nodes.statement: At a given time step $t$, we define the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ as the set containing all the matrices $H$ that are consistent with the Assumptions \ref{A:disturbance} and \ref{A:system_class} and the collected input-output data \eqref{Eq:measured_data}: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}(t)\!\doteq\! \left\{\begin{array}{ll} H\!\in\! \mathcal{F}(0)\!:\!&-\epsilon_d\!-\!\epsilon_v\leq \tilde{y}(l)\!-\!H\varphi(l)\leq \epsilon_d\!+\!\epsilon_v,\,\forall l \in [0,t] \end{array}\right\}\!\!. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
differentia: containing all the matrices $H$ that are consistent with the Assumptions \ref{A:disturbance} and \ref{A:system_class} and the collected input-output data \eqref{Eq:measured_data}

nodes.name: Polytopic structure of the model set
nodes.statement: Since the initial model set $\mathcal{F}(0)$ is defined by polytopic constraints on each row $H_j^T$ of the matrix $H$, and the constraints in \eqref{Eq:FSSm_t} are linear, the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ is still defined by polytopic constraints on $H_j^T,\, j=1,\hdots n_y$. Each of these polytopes can be uniquely described by a set of non-redundant inequalities.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: intersecting polytopes with linear (half-space) constraints keeps polytopes, each with a unique non-redundant H-representation.

nodes.name: Polytopic representation of the model set
nodes.statement: Therefore, at a generic time step $t$, the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ can be represented as: \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}(t)\!=\! \left\{H\!\in\!{\mathbb R}^{n_y \times n_um}\!:\!A_j(t)H_{j}\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y \right\}, \end{equation} where $A_j(t) \in {\mathbb R}^{r_j(t) \times n_um}$, $b_j(t) \in {\mathbb R}^{r_j(t)}$ and $r_j(t)$ is the number of non-redundant inequalities pertaining to the $j^\text{th}$ row of the matrix $H$.
conclusions: the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ can be represented as:

nodes.name: Row polytopes F_j(t)
nodes.statement: To this end, let us consider the following polytopes: \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}_j(t)=\{H_j\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um}: A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)\},\, j=1\hdots n_y. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Recursive polytope update
nodes.statement: We note that for each $j$, the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$ can be calculated recursively in time as the intersection of the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t-1)$ and the two half spaces defined by the newly measured plant output, $\tilde{y}_j(t)$: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \mathcal{F}_{j}(t)= &\mathcal{F}_{j}(t-1) \\ &\cap \{H_{j}\!\!\in\!{\mathbb R}^{n_um}\!:\!\varphi(t)^TH_{j}\leq \tilde{y}_j(t)\!+\!\epsilon_{d_j}\!+\!\epsilon_{v_j}\}\\ &\cap \{H_{j}\!\!\in\!{\mathbb R}^{n_um}\!:\! -\varphi(t)^TH_{j}\leq -\tilde{y}_j(t)\!+\!\epsilon_{d_j}\!+\!\epsilon_{v_j}\}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
conclusions: the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$ can be calculated recursively in time as the intersection of the polytope $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t-1)$ and the two half spaces defined by the newly measured plant output, $\tilde{y}_j(t)$:
nodes.statement_short: Each row polytope is updated by intersecting the previous one with the two half-spaces from the new measurement.

nodes.name: Redundancy removal and limited-complexity update
nodes.statement: The matrix $A_j(t)$ and the vector $b_j(t)$ can then be calculated by removing any redundant faces of the polytope $F_j(t)$. This can be done by solving an LP for each face of the polytope, in order to determine whether it is redundant or not \cite{Polytopi1}. A problem of the described recursive update is that the number of faces of $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$, $r_j(t)$, can become arbitrarily large, as in general it grows linearly with time, and hence the memory needed to store $A_j(t)$ and $b_j(t)$ can become impractical. In order to overcome this problem, limited complexity polytopic update algorithm similar to the one proposed in \cite{limited_poly_update} can be used.
nodes.statement_short: Remove redundant faces by one LP per face; since face count grows linearly, use a limited-complexity polytope update.

nodes.name: Nominal model (Chebyshev centers)
nodes.statement: In addition to the model set, the proposed SM identification algorithm also provides a nominal model of the plant (step 2) of Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2}). The latter is given by a matrix $H_{c}(t)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y\times n_um}$, $H_c=[H_{c,1},\hdots H_{c,n_y}]^T$, where $H_{c,j}(t)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um},\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ are computed as the centers of the maximum volume $l_2$-norm balls inscribed in the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: The nominal model $H_c(t)$ has rows equal to the centers of maximum-volume balls inscribed in the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_j(t)$.

nodes.name: Regularized central estimate LP
nodes.statement: This can be done by solving an LP, however the solution is not unique in general. Therefore, we introduce a regularization term, that penalizes the deviation of the new nominal model from the previous one, giving rise to the following LP: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{c} \max \limits_{\xi_j(t),H_{c,j}(t)} \sum \limits_{j=1}^{n_y}\xi_j(t)-\alpha\|H_{c,j}(t-1)-H_{c,j}(t)\|_1\\ \text{subject to}\\ a_{ji}(t)H_{c,j}(t)\!+\!\xi_j(t)\|a_{ji}(t)\|_2\!\leq\! b_{ji}(t), \, j=1,\hdots, n_y,\, i=1,\hdots, n_u, \end{array} \end{equation} where $\xi_j(t) \in {\mathbb R}$ is the radius of the maximum volume ball inscribed in $\mathcal{F}_{j}(t)$, $\alpha>0$ is a design variable, and $a_{ji}(t)$ and $b_{ji}(t)$ stand for the $i^{\text{th}}$ row of the matrix $A_j(t)$ and the vector $b_j(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: LP maximizing inscribed-ball radii minus an $\ell_1$ penalty on change of the nominal model.

nodes.name: Future control moves
nodes.statement: Let $u(k|t),\, k\in[t,t+N-1]$, $N\geq m$, be the possible future control moves, where the notation $k|t$ indicates the prediction at step $k\geq t$ given the information at the current step $t$.

nodes.name: Future input increments
nodes.statement: Similarly, we define the vectors of future input increments $\Delta u(k|t), \, k\in [t,t+N-1]$ as:

nodes.name: Future regressor vectors
nodes.statement: Moreover, we define the future regressor vectors $\varphi(k|t)\in{\mathbb R}^{n_um},\,k\in[t+1,t+N]$ as: \begin{equation} \varphi(k|t)\!=\!\!\begin{cases} W\varphi(t)\!\!+\!\!Zu(t|t)\!\!\! & \text{if} \,\, k=t+1\\ W \varphi(k\!-\!1|t)\!\!+\!\!Zu(k\!-\!1|t) \!\!\!& \text{if} \,\, t\!+\!2\!\leq\! k\!\leq\! t\!+\!N. \end{cases} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Current prediction error
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the current prediction error $\hat{d}(t)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_y}$ as the difference between the measured plant output and the one predicted by the nominal model at the time step $t$: \begin{equation} \hat{d}(t)\doteq \tilde{y}(t)-H_c(t)\varphi(t). \end{equation}

nodes.name: MPC cost function
nodes.statement: Then, we consider the following cost function: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} J(U,\tilde{y}(t),\varphi(t))\doteq \sum\limits_{k=t}^{t\!+\!N\!-\!1}\!&\!\left(\hat{y}(k\!+\!1|t)\!-\!y_{\text{des}}(k\!+\!1|t)\right)^TQ(\hat{y}(k\!+\!1|t)-\!y_{\text{des}}(k\!+\!1|t))\!+\! u(k|t)^TSu(k|t)\\&+\Delta u(k|t)^TR\Delta u(k|t), \end{aligned}\!\! \end{equation} where: \begin{equation} \hat{y}(k+1|t)=H_c(t)\varphi(k+1|t)+\hat{d}(t). \end{equation} In \eqref{Eq:cost_function}, $U=[u(t|t) \ldots u(t+N-1|t)]$ are the decision variables, while $\tilde{y}(t)$ and $\varphi(t)$ are known parameters. $y_\text{des}(k|t),\,k\in[t+1,t+N]$, are the predicted values of the desired output.
nodes.statement_short: Finite-horizon quadratic tracking cost on nominal-model predictions with disturbance estimate, plus input and input-rate penalties.

nodes.name: Offset-free tracking and consistency with the original objective
nodes.statement: The introduction of the disturbance estimate $\hat{d}(t)$ in the cost function enables offset free tracking. Moreover, if the nominal model of the plant $H_c(t)$ were equal to the real plant, the measurement noise $v(t)$ were zero, and the output disturbance $d(t)$ were constant, for $N=T$, minimizing the cost function \eqref{Eq:cost_function} would be equivalent to minimizing the cost function of the control objective \eqref{Eq:problem_cost}.

nodes.name: Disturbance-tightened output constraints
nodes.statement: The constraints \eqref{Eq:output1} are satisfied for anny disturbance realization if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \begin{equation} EH\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d}\leq p, \, \forall H\! \in\! \mathcal{F}(t),\, \forall k\in[t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N], \end{equation} where $\overline{d}=[\overline{d}_1,\hdots, \overline{d}_{n_o}]^T$, and $d_l \in {\mathbb R},\, l=1,\hdots, n_o$ are given as: \begin{equation} \overline{d}_l=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}|e_{lj}|\epsilon_{d_j}, \end{equation} where $e_{lj}$ stand for the element of the $l^\text{th}$ row and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E$.
assumptions: the following set of inequalities is satisfied:
conclusions: The constraints \eqref{Eq:output1} are satisfied for anny disturbance realization
nodes.statement_short: Robust output constraints hold for every bounded disturbance if the nominal constraints are tightened by $\overline{d}_l=\sum_j|e_{lj}|\epsilon_{d_j}$.

nodes.name: Linear reformulation of robust output constraints
nodes.statement: The constraints (\ref{Eq:output}) are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is feasible: \small \begin{equation} \left.\begin{array}{l}\!\! A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[\begin{array}{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t) \end{array}\right]\\ b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l\\ \lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 \end{array} \right\}\begin{array}{cc}\forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\ \forall k\!\in\![t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N]\end{array} \end{equation} \normalsize with \small \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} A(t)&=\left[\begin{array}{cccc} A_1(t)& \bold 0& \ldots&\bold 0\\ \bold 0& A_2(t)& \ldots& \bold 0\\ \vdots& \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \bold 0&\bold 0& \ldots&A_{n_y}(t)\end{array} \right]\\ b(t)&=\left[\begin{array}{c} b_1(t)\\ \vdots\\ b_{n_y}(t) \end{array} \right], \end{aligned} \end{equation} \normalsize where $\bold 0$ represents zero matrices of appropriate dimensions and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E$ and $p_l$ is the $l^\text{th}$ element of the vector $p$. In \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}, $\lambda_l(k|t) \in {\mathbb R}^{r(t)}$ are additional decision variables, where $r(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_y} r_j(t)$.
assumptions: $\lambda_l(k|t) \in {\mathbb R}^{r(t)}$ are additional decision variables, where $r(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{n_y} r_j(t)$
conclusions: The constraints (\ref{Eq:output}) are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is feasible:
nodes.statement_short: Robust output constraints over the polytopic model set hold iff a finite set of LP-dual feasibility constraints in $\lambda_l(k|t)$ is feasible.
nodes.label: L:constraint_equivalence_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: We first note that, from the definition of the set $\mathcal{F}(t)$, it follows that constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} \gamma_l(k)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l, & \begin{array}{c} \forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\\forall k\in [t+1,t+N]\end{array}\end{array} \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \gamma_l(k)=\max \limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}\varphi(k|t)^TH_j. \end{equation} For fixed values of the vectors $\varphi(k|t), \, k\in [t+1,t+N]$, by using the fact that the inequalities $A_j(t) H_j\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ form nonempty, closed and bounded convex sets (i.e. polytopes), we can write the dual of the LP \eqref{Eq:Linear_proggrams_1} as: \begin{eqnarray} &\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\min \limits_{\lambda_l(k|t)}b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\\ &\text{subject to} \nonumber\\ &A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[ \begin{array}{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t)\end{array}\right]\\ &\lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 . \end{eqnarray} According to the strong duality theorem for LPs \cite{LP_book}, it holds that: $\gamma_l(k)=\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)$. Therefore, for any $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfies the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1c1}) and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2}, it holds that $\gamma_l(k) \leq b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)$. Hence the existence of $\varphi(k|t)$ and $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfy the set of constraints (\ref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}) guarantees that the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1}) are also satisfied, which implies the satisfaction of the original constraints \eqref{Eq:output}. On the other hand if the constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied, then there exists $\gamma_l(k)$ satisfying \eqref{Eq:LP1}. Then by the strong duality theorem for LP, $\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\gamma_l(k)$ exists and hence the constraints \eqref{Eq:LP1c1} and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2} have to be feasible, which implies the feasibility of \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}. \hfill$\blacksquare$
nodes.statement_short: LP duality: write the worst-case output as an LP, take its dual, and use strong duality to show both directions of the equivalence.

nodes.name: Finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP)
nodes.statement: For fixed values of $N$, $Q$, $S$ and $R$, we can now define the finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) to be solved at time step $t$ (see step 3) of Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2}): \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \min \limits_{U} &J(U,\tilde{y}(t),\varphi (t))\\ &\text{subject to}\, \eqref{Eq:input_rate},\, \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} which is a quadratic program (QP), that can be efficiently solved.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the MPC cost subject to input constraints, dual-LP robust output constraints and the terminal steady-state constraint; a QP.

nodes.name: Recursive feasibility of the adaptive MPC
nodes.statement: The proposed adaptive control algorithm is such that if the problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} that is solved under Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2} has a feasible solution at time step $0$, then it is guaranteed to have a feasible solution $\forall t\geq 0$. This means that the proposed adaptive control algorithm guarantees the satisfaction of both input and output constraints $\forall t$.
assumptions: if the problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} that is solved under Algorithm \ref{Alg:RHCOP2} has a feasible solution at time step $0$
conclusions: then it is guaranteed to have a feasible solution $\forall t\geq 0$
the proposed adaptive control algorithm guarantees the satisfaction of both input and output constraints $\forall t$

nodes.name: Two-stage exploring control input computation
nodes.statement: A possible method to add an exploring property to the control algorithm is to split the calculation of the control input in two stages. In the first stage, the FHOCP \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} is solved as usual. The computed optimal control sequence and the knowledge of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ are then used to calculate the upper bounds, along the chosen prediction horizon, on the absolute difference between all the possible future outputs of the plant and the nominal optimal output trajectory. In the second stage, by allowing these bounds to be inflated by a factor selected by the control designer, the sequence of control inputs can then be recalculated in order to improve the reduction in size of the model set. To this end, the control input is selected such that it approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set at the next time step, while at the same time ensuring that the difference between the future trajectory of the plant outputs and the optimal one calculated in the first stage remains inside the selected bounds, and that the input and output constraints are satisfied.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Two stages: solve the FHOCP, bound output deviations over the model set, then re-solve to shrink the next model set within inflated bounds.

nodes.name: Automatic trade-off between tracking and identification
nodes.statement: With this approach, the relative importance of reference tracking and identification is automatically linked to the amount of information available on the system, which is represented by the size of the model set. In fact, if the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ is large, the input and trajectories computed at the second stage will be allowed to significantly deviate from the ones calculated in the first stage, in order to generate a control input that is informative and reduces the size of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$. On the other hand, if the uncertainty is small, the future plant output will be allowed to change only slightly from the first to the second stage.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Large model sets let the second stage deviate strongly to explore; small ones allow only slight changes.

nodes.name: First-stage predicted regressors and outputs
nodes.statement: We denote the predicted regressor vectors and plant outputs obtained by solving \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} by $\varphi'(k|t)$ and $\hat{y}'(k|t),\, k\in[t+1,t+N]$.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Output deviation bounds
nodes.statement: Then for the second stage, we compute the following quantities: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)=&\max \left\{ \overline{y}_j(k|t)-\hat{y}'_j(k|t),\, \hat{y}'_j(k|t)-\underline{y}_j(k|t) \right \}, k\in [t+1,t+N],\,\, j=1,\hdots, n_y, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)=[\overline{\epsilon}_1(k|t),\hdots, \overline{\epsilon}_{n_y}(k|t)]^T$, $\overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)\geq 0$ denotes the maximal possible difference between the possible future output of the plant and the predicted output at time step $k$, and \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ccc} \overline{y}_j(k|t)&=&\max\limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)} H_j^T\varphi'(k|t)\\ \underline{y}_j(k|t)&=& \min\limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)} H_j^T\varphi'(k|t). \end{array} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{\epsilon}_j(k|t)$ is the maximal deviation of any model-set output from the first-stage prediction.

nodes.name: Regressor matrix Phi(t+1|t)
nodes.statement: In addition, we define the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um\times n_um}$ that depends on the $n_um$ past regressor vectors and the first future regressor vector as: \begin{equation} \Phi(t+1|t)=\left[\begin{array}{cccc} \varphi(t-n_um+1) &\hdots & \varphi(t) & \varphi(t+1|t) \end{array} \right]. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm

nodes.name: Volume bound on the updated polytopes
nodes.statement: Each of the polytopes $\mathcal{F}_j(t+1),\, j=1,\hdots,n_y$ obtained by using the polytopic update of the form \eqref{Eq:Normal_update} for a sequence of control input vectors that define the regressor vectors forming the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ is guaranteed to have the volume smaller than $\frac{\left(2(\epsilon_{d_j}+\epsilon_{v_j})\right)^{n_um}}{\left| \det\left( \Phi(t+1|t)\right)\right|}$.\hfill$\blacksquare$
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
assumptions: obtained by using the polytopic update of the form \eqref{Eq:Normal_update} for a sequence of control input vectors that define the regressor vectors forming the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$
conclusions: is guaranteed to have the volume smaller than $\frac{\left(2(\epsilon_{d_j}+\epsilon_{v_j})\right)^{n_um}}{\left| \det\left( \Phi(t+1|t)\right)\right|}$
nodes.statement_short: The volume of each updated polytope is at most $(2(\epsilon_{d_j}+\epsilon_{v_j}))^{n_um}/|\det\Phi(t+1|t)|$.
nodes.label: L:volume

nodes.name: Second-stage exploring problem
nodes.statement: The input to be applied to the plant is selected within a set of all the control inputs that satisfy input and output constraints and that keep all of the possible predicted output trajectories inside an interval obtained by scaling the values of $\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)$, centered at the trajectory $\hat{y}'(k|t),\, k\in[t+1,t+N]$. In order to improve the knowledge on the system, we need a suitable cost function that penalizes the size of the model set. By considering the result of \cite{id_aspect}, we chose to consider $|\det(\Phi(t+1|t))|$ and compute an input that increases its value. Therefore, the optimization problem to be solved at the second stage of the control input calculation is given as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\max \limits_U \left|\det \Phi(t+1|t) \right|\\ &\text {subject to}\\ &\eqref{Eq:input_rate}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint},\\ &\left.\begin{array}{lll} H\varphi(k|t)&\!\leq\!& \hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\ H\varphi(k|t)&\!\geq\! &\hat{y}'(k|t)\!-\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\ EH\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d}&\! \leq\!&\! p \end{array} \right\}\begin{array}{ll}\forall H\in \mathcal{F}(t)\\ \forall k\in[t\!+\!1, t\!+\!N] \end{array} \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $r\in {\mathbb R}$, $r\geq 1$ is a design parameter, selected by the control designer, that determines the allowed augmentation of the intervals containing the predicted outputs between the first and second stages. This parameter indicates by how much the bounds \eqref{Eq:bounds1} are allowed to be inflated.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Maximize $|\det\Phi(t+1|t)|$ subject to input constraints, terminal constraint, robust output constraints and inflated output-deviation bounds.

nodes.name: Linear reformulation of the second-stage constraints
nodes.statement: However, in this specific case the infinite dimensional constraints can be reformulated into a set of linear constraints.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
conclusions: the infinite dimensional constraints can be reformulated into a set of linear constraints

nodes.name: Reformulation via augmented matrices and Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: In fact, if we define the matrix $E''$ and the vectors $\overline{d''}$ and $p''(k|t),\, k\in [t+1,t+N]$ as: \begin{equation} E''=\left[ \begin{array}{c} I\\ -I\\ E \end{array} \right],\, \overline{d''}=\left[\begin{array}{c} \bold{0}\\ \bold{0}\\ \overline{d} \end{array} \right],\, p''(k|t)=\left[ \begin{array}{c} \hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\-\hat{y}'(k|t)\!+\!r\overline{\epsilon}(k|t)\\p\end{array} \right], \end{equation} where $I$ and $\bold{0}$ respectively denote the identity and zero matrices of apropriate size, then the infinite dimensional constraints in \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can be rewritten as \begin{equation} E''H\varphi(k|t)\!+\!\overline{d''}\leq p''(k|t),\, \forall H\in \mathcal{F}(t),\, k\in[t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N], \end{equation} and these constraints can be written in the form of linear constraints by using the Lemma \ref{L:constraint_equivalence_1}.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Stack the deviation-bound and output constraints into $E''$, $\overline{d''}$, $p''$ and apply Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: Determinant is affine in the first future input
nodes.statement: In addition, we note that from the definition of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ and the regressor vector $\varphi(t+1|t)$, it follows that the determinant of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ can be expressed as a linear function of the first future control input as: \begin{equation} \det\left(\Phi(t+1|t)\right)=k^T u(t|t)+n, \end{equation} where the derivation of $k \in {\mathbb R}^{n_u}$ and $n \in {\mathbb R}$ is given in the Appendix \ref{S:alpha_beta}.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
assumptions: from the definition of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ and the regressor vector $\varphi(t+1|t)$
conclusions: the determinant of the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ can be expressed as a linear function of the first future control input as:

nodes.name: Two LPs for the second stage
nodes.statement: Therefore, the optimization problem \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can be solved by first solving the following two LPs: \begin{eqnarray} J_1=\max \limits_{u(k|t)} k^T u(t|t)\\ J_2=\min \limits_{u(k|t)} k^T u(t|t) \end{eqnarray} \begin{equation} \begin{array}{l} \text{subject to}\\ \eqref{Eq:input_rate}, \, \eqref{Eq:end_constraint},\\ \left.\begin{array}{l}\!\! A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[\begin{array}{c} e_{l1}''\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}''\varphi(k|t) \end{array}\right]\\ b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\leq p_l''(k|t)\!-\!\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}''\epsilon_{d_j}\\ \lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 \end{array}\!\!\! \right\}\begin{array}{cc}\forall l=1,\!\hdots,\!n_o\!+\!2n_y\\ \forall k\!\in\![t\!+\!1,t\!+\!N]\end{array} \end{array} \end{equation} where $e_{lj}''$ stand for the element of the $l^\text{th}$ row and $j^\text{th}$ column of the matrix $E''$ and $p_l''(k|t)$ is the $l^\text{th}$ element of the vector $p''(k|t)$. The matrix $A(t)$ and the vector $b(t)$ are defined as in \eqref{Eq:explanation}.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Maximize and minimize $k^T u(t|t)$ subject to input, terminal and dual-LP robust constraints.

nodes.name: Second-stage solution from the two LPs
nodes.statement: The solution to \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} can then be obtained by comparing the cost function values of the two LPs: if $|J_1+n|\leq |J_2+n|$, then the solution of the LP with the cost function \eqref{Eq:cost1} is the solution of the original problem and vice-versa.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
conclusions: then the solution of the LP with the cost function \eqref{Eq:cost1} is the solution of the original problem and vice-versa

nodes.name: Recursive feasibility of the exploring extension
nodes.statement: Moreover, the optimization problem that is solved in the second stage of the control input calculation is guaranteed to be recursively feasible, since the solution obtained in the first stage is always a feasible solution for the second stage. Due to this, the proposed extension allows us to retain the guarantee of constraint satisfaction for all time.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
assumptions: since the solution obtained in the first stage is always a feasible solution for the second stage
conclusions: the optimization problem that is solved in the second stage of the control input calculation is guaranteed to be recursively feasible
the proposed extension allows us to retain the guarantee of constraint satisfaction for all time

nodes.name: Approximate nature of the volume minimization
nodes.statement: The cost function \eqref{Eq:FHOCP2_cost} only approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set in the next time step. In order to have exact minimization, all the collected control inputs and the effects of the limited polytopic update algorithm would need to be taken into account. However, the resulting optimization problem would then be computationally intractable. In addition, the cost function minimizes only the volume of the polytopes in the next time step and not over the whole prediction horizon, as this would also lead to a computationally intractable optimization problem. Despite these approximations, the proposed modification gives good results in practice, as shown by the numerical example.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: The determinant cost only approximately and one-step-ahead minimizes model-set volume; exact versions are intractable.
nodes.label: R:note_on_complexity

nodes.name: Block w for impulse response parametrization
nodes.statement: For the case when impulse response parametrization is used ($\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ is given by \eqref{Eq:impulse_response}), we define the matrix $w\in {\mathbb R}^{n_u \times n_u}$ with the following structure: \begin{equation*} w=\left[ \begin{array}{ccccc} 0 & 0 & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ a & 0 & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ 0 & a & \hdots & 0 & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots\\ 0 & 0 & \hdots & a & 0 \end{array} \right] \in {\mathbb R}^{m\times m}.

nodes.name: Matrix W
nodes.statement: Based on this, the matrix $W$ is given by: \begin{equation} W=\left[\begin{array}{cccc} w &\bold{0} & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \bold{0} & w & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \bold{0} & \bold{0} & \hdots & w \end{array}\right] \in {\mathbb R}^{n_um \times n_um}, \end{equation} where $\bold{0}$ denotes the matrix of all zeros with appropriate dimension.

nodes.name: Matrix Z
nodes.statement: Similarly, in order to define the matrix $Z\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um\times n_u}$, we first define the vector $z=[a,0,\hdots,0]^T\in {\mathbb R}^m$. Then we can write the matrix $Z$ as: \begin{equation} Z=\left[\begin{array}{cccc} z & \bold{0} & \hdots & \bold{0}\\ \bold{0} & z & \hdots & \bold {0}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \bold{0} & \bold{0} & \hdots & z \end{array} \right]\in {\mathbb R}^{n_um\times n_u}, \end{equation} where $\bold{0}$ denotes the vector of all zeros of dimension $m$.

nodes.name: Regressor matrices for Laguerre parametrization
nodes.statement: For the case when Laguerre basis functions are used for parametrization ($\mathcal{L}_k(a,q)$ is given by \eqref{Eq:Laguere}), we define the matrix $w \in {\mathbb R}^{m\times m}$ as: \begin{equation*} w=\left[\begin{array}{ccccc} a & 0 & 0 & \hdots & 0\\ 1-a^2 & a & 0 &\hdots & 0\\ (-a)(1-a^2) & 1-a^2 & a & \hdots & 0\\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ (-a)^{m-2}(1-a^2) & (-a)^{m-3}(1-a^2)& \hdots &\hdots& a \end{array} \right]. \end{equation*} The matrix $W$ is then defined as in \eqref{Eq:W}. The vector $z\in {\mathbb R}^m$ is defined as: \begin{equation*} z=\sqrt{1-a^2}\left[\begin{array}{c} 1\\-a\\(-a)^2\\ \hdots \\ (-a)^{m-1} \end{array} \right]\in {\mathbb R}^m, \end{equation*} and $Z$ is given as in \eqref{Eq:Z}.
nodes.statement_short: Laguerre-case $w$ (lower-triangular with $a$ and $(-a)^i(1-a^2)$) and $z=\sqrt{1-a^2}[1,-a,\dots]^T$, giving $W$ and $Z$.

nodes.name: Derivation of k and n
nodes.statement: In order to define $k \in {\mathbb R}^{n_u}$ and $n \in {\mathbb R}$, we first shortly recall the definition of the matrix determinant. For a square matrix $A\in {\mathbb R}^{N\times N}$, the determinant is defined as: \begin{equation} \det (A)=\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_N}\mbox {\rm sgn }(\sigma) \prod \limits_{i=1}^N A_{i,\sigma_i}, \end{equation} where $S_N$ denotes the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,N\}$, $\mbox {\rm sgn } (\sigma)$ returns $1$ if the permutation $\sigma$ is even and $-1$ if the permutation is odd and $A_{i,\sigma_i}$ denotes the element of the matrix $A$ in the $i^{\text{th}}$ row and the column defined by the $i^{\text{th}}$ element in the permutation $\sigma$.\\ We rewrite the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ as $\Phi(t+1|t)=\left[\Phi',\, W\varphi(t)+Zu(t|t)\right]$, where \begin{equation*} \Phi'=\left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \Phi_{1,1} &\hdots & \Phi_{1,n_um-1}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \Phi_{n_um,1}& \hdots & \Phi_{n_um,n_um-1} \end{array} \right], \end{equation*} with the elements $\Phi_{p,q}\in {\mathbb R},\,\, p=1,\hdots,n_um,\, q=1,\hdots,n_um-1$, denoting the corresponding elements of the applied regerssor vectors $\varphi(k),\, k=t-n_um+1,\hdots, t-1$. In addition, we denote by $S_{n_um}^i,\, i=1,\hdots, n_um$ the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,n_um\}$ that have $n_um$ at the $i^{\text{th}}$ position. Based on this we define the vector $V \in {\mathbb R}^{n_um}$ as: \begin{equation} V=\left[ \begin{array}{c} \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^1} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^2} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=1,\,i\neq 2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \vdots \\\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^{n_um}} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{ i=1,\, i\neq n_um}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\end{array} \right]. \end{equation} Then we can express $k$ and $n$ by using $V$ as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} k^T&=V^TZ\\ n&=V^TW\varphi(t). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\det\Phi(t+1|t)$ by the Leibniz formula along the last column $W\varphi(t)+Zu(t|t)$, collecting cofactor sums into $V$.

nodes.name: Reduce to worst-case LP values
nodes.statement: We first note that, from the definition of the set $\mathcal{F}(t)$, it follows that constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied if and only if the following set of inequalities is satisfied: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{ll} \gamma_l(k)\leq p_l\!-\!\overline{d}_l, & \begin{array}{c} \forall l=1,\hdots,n_o\\\forall k\in [t+1,t+N]\end{array}\end{array} \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \gamma_l(k)=\max \limits_{A_j(t)H_j\leq b_j(t)}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n_y}e_{lj}\varphi(k|t)^TH_j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the robust constraints to bounds on LP optimal values $\gamma_l(k)$.

nodes.name: Write the dual LP
nodes.statement: For fixed values of the vectors $\varphi(k|t), \, k\in [t+1,t+N]$, by using the fact that the inequalities $A_j(t) H_j\leq b_j(t),\, j=1,\hdots, n_y$ form nonempty, closed and bounded convex sets (i.e. polytopes), we can write the dual of the LP \eqref{Eq:Linear_proggrams_1} as: \begin{eqnarray} &\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\min \limits_{\lambda_l(k|t)}b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)\\ &\text{subject to} \nonumber\\ &A(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)=\left[ \begin{array}{c} e_{l1}\varphi(k|t)\\ \vdots\\ e_{ln_y}\varphi(k|t)\end{array}\right]\\ &\lambda_l(k|t)\geq \bold 0 . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Form the dual LP of the worst-case output problem.

nodes.name: Apply strong duality
nodes.statement: According to the strong duality theorem for LPs \cite{LP_book}, it holds that: $\gamma_l(k)=\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)$. Therefore, for any $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfies the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1c1}) and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2}, it holds that $\gamma_l(k) \leq b(t)^T\lambda_l(k|t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong duality gives $\gamma_l=\tilde\gamma_l$, so every dual-feasible $\lambda$ upper bounds $\gamma_l$.

nodes.name: Sufficiency
nodes.statement: Hence the existence of $\varphi(k|t)$ and $\lambda_l(k|t)$ that satisfy the set of constraints (\ref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}) guarantees that the constraints (\ref{Eq:LP1}) are also satisfied, which implies the satisfaction of the original constraints \eqref{Eq:output}.
nodes.statement_short: Feasibility of the dual constraints implies the robust output constraints.

nodes.name: Necessity
nodes.statement: On the other hand if the constraints \eqref{Eq:output} are satisfied, then there exists $\gamma_l(k)$ satisfying \eqref{Eq:LP1}. Then by the strong duality theorem for LP, $\tilde{\gamma}_l(k)=\gamma_l(k)$ exists and hence the constraints \eqref{Eq:LP1c1} and \eqref{Eq:LP1c2} have to be feasible, which implies the feasibility of \eqref{Eq:relaxed_constraints1}. \hfill$\blacksquare$
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, strong duality yields a feasible dual multiplier.

nodes.name: Recall determinant
nodes.statement: In order to define $k \in {\mathbb R}^{n_u}$ and $n \in {\mathbb R}$, we first shortly recall the definition of the matrix determinant. For a square matrix $A\in {\mathbb R}^{N\times N}$, the determinant is defined as: \begin{equation} \det (A)=\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_N}\mbox {\rm sgn }(\sigma) \prod \limits_{i=1}^N A_{i,\sigma_i}, \end{equation} where $S_N$ denotes the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,N\}$, $\mbox {\rm sgn } (\sigma)$ returns $1$ if the permutation $\sigma$ is even and $-1$ if the permutation is odd and $A_{i,\sigma_i}$ denotes the element of the matrix $A$ in the $i^{\text{th}}$ row and the column defined by the $i^{\text{th}}$ element in the permutation $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Leibniz formula for the determinant.

nodes.name: Split Phi and define V
nodes.statement: We rewrite the matrix $\Phi(t+1|t)$ as $\Phi(t+1|t)=\left[\Phi',\, W\varphi(t)+Zu(t|t)\right]$, where \begin{equation*} \Phi'=\left[ \begin{array}{ccc} \Phi_{1,1} &\hdots & \Phi_{1,n_um-1}\\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ \Phi_{n_um,1}& \hdots & \Phi_{n_um,n_um-1} \end{array} \right], \end{equation*} with the elements $\Phi_{p,q}\in {\mathbb R},\,\, p=1,\hdots,n_um,\, q=1,\hdots,n_um-1$, denoting the corresponding elements of the applied regerssor vectors $\varphi(k),\, k=t-n_um+1,\hdots, t-1$. In addition, we denote by $S_{n_um}^i,\, i=1,\hdots, n_um$ the set of all the permutations of the integers $\{1,\hdots,n_um\}$ that have $n_um$ at the $i^{\text{th}}$ position. Based on this we define the vector $V \in {\mathbb R}^{n_um}$ as: \begin{equation} V=\left[ \begin{array}{c} \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^1} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^2} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{i=1,\,i\neq 2}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\\ \vdots \\\sum \limits_{\sigma \in S_{n_um}^{n_um}} sgn(\sigma) \prod\limits_{ i=1,\, i\neq n_um}^{n_um}\Phi_{i,\sigma_i}\end{array} \right]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Separate the last column $W\varphi(t)+Zu(t|t)$ and define cofactor sums $V$.

nodes.name: Express k and n
nodes.statement: Then we can express $k$ and $n$ by using $V$ as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} k^T&=V^TZ\\ n&=V^TW\varphi(t). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Read off $k^T=V^TZ$ and $n=V^TW\varphi(t)$.

nodes.name: Update model set
nodes.statement: [1)]At time step $t$, obtain $\tilde{y}(t)$ and update the model set based on the past applied control inputs and measured plant outputs;
nodes.statement_short: Measure output and refine the set-membership model set.

nodes.name: Select nominal model
nodes.statement: [2)] Select a nominal model of the plant inside the model set;
nodes.statement_short: Pick the nominal model.

nodes.name: Solve FHOCP
nodes.statement: [3)]Calculate a sequence of possible future control inputs by solving a finite horizon optimal control problem (FHOCP) that minimizes the weighted $l_2$ norm of the tracking error for the nominal model and enforces input and output constraints for all the models inside the model set;
nodes.statement_short: Solve the robust finite-horizon problem.

nodes.name: Apply first input and repeat
nodes.statement: [4)]Apply the first element of the calculated input sequence, set $t=t+1$, go to 1).
nodes.statement_short: Receding horizon: apply first input, advance time, loop.

nodes.name: First stage: solve FHOCP
nodes.statement: In the first stage, the FHOCP \eqref{Eq:FHOCP} is solved as usual.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Solve the standard FHOCP.

nodes.name: Compute output deviation bounds
nodes.statement: The computed optimal control sequence and the knowledge of the model set $\mathcal{F}(t)$ are then used to calculate the upper bounds, along the chosen prediction horizon, on the absolute difference between all the possible future outputs of the plant and the nominal optimal output trajectory.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Bound deviations of all model-set outputs from the nominal trajectory.

nodes.name: Second stage: recompute exploring input
nodes.statement: In the second stage, by allowing these bounds to be inflated by a factor selected by the control designer, the sequence of control inputs can then be recalculated in order to improve the reduction in size of the model set. To this end, the control input is selected such that it approximately minimizes the volume of the polytopes that will form the model set at the next time step, while at the same time ensuring that the difference between the future trajectory of the plant outputs and the optimal one calculated in the first stage remains inside the selected bounds, and that the input and output constraints are satisfied.
nodes.section: 5 Adding an exploring property to the control algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Re-solve to approximately minimize next model-set volume within inflated bounds and constraints.
